prompt: In the uncompensated ideal ladder model, turning up resonance weakens the lowest bass even while a peak grows near the stage corner. Why?

options.text: The negative feedback also reduces low-frequency gain
options.explanation: Correct. At DC each stage passes the signal, so the loop’s negative feedback suppresses the overall low-frequency response.

options.text: Resonance can affect only a single frequency, so the observation is impossible
options.explanation: Feedback changes the whole transfer response, including low-frequency gain.

options.text: The filter converts bass into a higher-pitched note at every setting
options.explanation: The fixed linear model changes amplitude and phase, not input frequencies.

options.text: A marginal linear threshold predicts the exact final self-oscillation amplitude
options.explanation: A marginal linear model does not bound the amplitude; real nonlinearities do.

workedExample: Follow a slowly varying signal through the stages: each passes it nearly unchanged, but some output is fed back negatively to the input. Stronger feedback therefore lowers the overall bass gain. Near the stage corner, accumulated phase changes the loop behaviour and produces resonance; real self-oscillation needs amplitude-limiting nonlinearities.
